slides.0.title: Introducing Argentine wine
slides.0.subtitle: Colonial origins, the story of Malbec and modernisation since the 1990s
slides.1.title: From colonial vines to the railway
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The earliest vines
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Father Juan Cedrón is credited with planting the first vines in 1556; sources differ on the place (Santiago del Estero, or the San Juan / Mendoza area). Planting in Mendoza expanded in the early 1560s
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Pouget and Malbec
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget brought French cuttings, including Argentina's first Malbec, at the request of Domingo Faustino Sarmiento; Wine With Seth dates this to 1853, while other sources give no year
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The railway of 1885
slides.1.highlights.2.content: The railway between Mendoza and Buenos Aires was completed in 1885, carrying Mendoza's wine to the main consumer market
slides.1.content: Argentine wine history begins with church vineyards in the colonial era; French varieties and the railway industrialised it in the 19th century.
slides.2.title: From a home market to the world stage
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The era of volume over quality
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Production peaked in 1977 with little focus on quality; Mendoza's vineyard area fell from about 254,891 ha in 1980 to about 146,080 ha in 2003
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The 1990s turn-around
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Exports began to grow, and "flying winemakers" brought yield control, temperature-controlled fermentation and new oak; the 2002 peso devaluation gave the industry and wine tourism another boost
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Catena and high-altitude Malbec
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Nicolás Catena planted the Adrianna Vineyard at about 1,450–1,500 m in Gualtallary, Tupungato (sources say 1992 or 1994), setting the direction for high-altitude Malbec
slides.2.content: The 1990s were the turning point: from bulk production to quality and exports, with the eyes turning to higher altitudes.
slides.3.title: Argentina today
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Scale
slides.3.highlights.0.content: About 220,000 ha of vineyards (Wine With Seth, year not given); red wine makes up nearly 60% of production
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Main provinces
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Mendoza accounts for over half of national output (sources say "more than 60%" or "more than two-thirds"), followed by San Juan
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The national drink
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Wine was declared Argentina's national drink in 2010 (the law cited by Wikipedia is dated 2013)
slides.3.content: Today's Argentina is centred on Mendoza, is mostly red, and is represented by Malbec.
Who brought the first Malbec cuttings to Argentina?
Pouget brought them at Sarmiento's request; Sarmiento was the one who asked, not the one who brought them.

Which was NOT among the practices brought by "flying winemakers" in the 1990s?
